solutions.explanation:
The signs alternate on the even-indexed binomial coefficients. These are exactly the signs produced by even powers of the imaginary unit \(i\), where \(i^2=-1\):
\[
i^{2k}=(-1)^k.
\]
Odd powers of \(i\) are \(i\) or \(-i\), so they have zero real part.

Let \(S\) denote the requested sum. By the binomial theorem,
\[
(1+i)^{99}=\sum_{j=0}^{99}\binom{99}{j}i^j.
\]
Taking the real part keeps exactly the even-indexed terms, giving
\[
S=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((1+i)^{99}\bigr),
\]
where \(\operatorname{Re}\) means the real part.

To compute this power, first find a small power that is real:
\[
(1+i)^2=2i,
\qquad (1+i)^4=-4.
\]
Also,
\[
(1+i)^3=2i(1+i)=-2+2i.
\]
Since \(99=4\cdot24+3\), we can group the factors as
\[
\begin{aligned}
(1+i)^{99}
&=\bigl((1+i)^4\bigr)^{24}(1+i)^3\\
&=(-4)^{24}(-2+2i)\\
&=2^{48}(-2+2i).
\end{aligned}
\]
Its real part is \(-2\cdot2^{48}\). Therefore
\[
S=\boxed{-2^{49}},
\]
choice B.
solutions.title: Read the sum from a complex binomial expansion
